[patient] okay .

[doctor] okay , all right . well , i'm glad to hear that . and you're taking your medication ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] okay , good . and any symptoms like chest pains , shortness of breath , any swelling in your legs ?
[patient] no , not that i've noticed .
[doctor] okay , all right . and then in terms of your depression , i know that we tried to stay off of medication in the past because you're on medications for your other problems . how are you doing ? and i know that you enrolled into therapy . is that helping ? or-
[patient] yeah , it's been helping a lot . i've been going every week , um , for the past year since my last annual exam . and that's been really helpful for me .
[doctor] okay . so , no , no issues , no feelings of wanting to harm yourself or hurt others ?
[patient] no , nothing like that .
[doctor] okay , all right . and then in terms of your high blood pressure , i know that you and i have kind of battled in the past with you remembering to take some of your blood pressure medications . how are you doing with that ?

[doctor] okay . and , and so how has work going for you ?
[patient] it's been okay . it's been a lot of long hours , late nights . a lot of , um , you know , fiscal year end data that i've been having to pull . so , a lot of responsibility , which is good . but with the responsibility comes the stress .

[patient] no , nothing like that .

[patient] okay .

[patient] okay .

[patient] okay .

[patient] okay .
[doctor] i also wan na repeat another echocardiogram , okay ?
[patient] all right .
[doctor] hey , dragon , order an echocardiogram . from a depression standpoint , it sounds like you're doing really well with that . so , i'm , i'm really happy for you . i'm , i'm glad to see that you're in therapy and you're doing really well . i do n't feel the need to start you on any medications this year , unless you feel differently .
[patient] no , i feel the same way .
[doctor] okay , all right . and then for your last problem your hypertension , you know , again i , i , i think it's out of control . but we'll see , i think , you know , i'd like to see you take the lisinopril as directed , okay ? uh , i want you to record your blood pressures within the patient , you know , take your blood pressure every day . record them to me for like , about a week , so i have to see if we have to add another agent , okay ? 'cause we need to get that under better control for your heart failure to be more successful , okay ?
[patient] okay .

[patient] okay .
[doctor] okay . do you have any questions ?
[patient] can i take all my pills at the same time ?
[doctor] yeah .
[patient] 'cause i've been trying to take them at different times of the day , 'cause i did n't know if it was bad to take them all at once or i should separate them . i do n't know .
[doctor] yeah . you can certainly take them , you know , all at the same time , as long , as yeah , they're all one scale . you can take them all at the same time . just set an alarm-
[patient] okay .
[doctor] . some time during the day to take them , okay ?
[patient] that might help me remember better .
[doctor] all right . that sounds good . all right , well , it's good to see you .
[patient] good seeing you too .
[doctor] hey , dragon , finalize the note .

VISIT NOTE (draft)

**Patient:** Martha, 50-year-old female
**Visit type:** Annual exam
**Clinician:** [doctor]

**PMH:** Congestive heart failure, depression, hypertension

**Subjective:**
- Feels well. Has been traveling and hiking, including the Mount Baker area in the Northern Cascades last weekend. Recently received a vaccine and feels safer traveling.
- CHF: Reports good adherence to a low-sodium diet, avoiding salty foods such as tater tots and soft pretzels. Reports taking medications. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, and leg swelling she has noticed.
- Depression: Attending weekly therapy for the past year, which she reports is helping a lot. Denies thoughts of harming self or others.
- Hypertension: Reports still forgetting to take blood pressure medication. Notes her blood pressure rises during stressful periods at work. Work involves long hours, late nights, and fiscal year-end data pulls, with significant responsibility and stress.
- ROS: Nasal congestion from fall pollen/allergies, per intake sheet. Denies nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

**Objective:**
- Blood pressure in office: elevated (numeric value not stated in transcript). Past readings reviewed and running on the higher side.
- Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted.
- Lower extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally. *(Transcript says "one plus pitting edema" without specifying laterality; please verify.)*
- Remainder of physical exam documented as normal per clinician.
- Echocardiogram (last year): LVEF approximately 45% ("low-ish" pumping function); mitral regurgitation, correlating with the murmur.
- Lipid panel (last year): cholesterol slightly elevated.

**Assessment and Plan:**

1. **Congestive heart failure**
   - Continue current medications.
   - Increase lisinopril to 40 mg daily, due to elevated blood pressure and mild fluid retention.
   - Start furosemide (Lasix) 20 mg daily.
   - Continue low-sodium diet.
   - Repeat echocardiogram (ordered).

2. **Depression**
   - Doing well with therapy. No new medication this year, per patient preference.

3. **Hypertension**
   - Assessed as not well controlled.
   - Take lisinopril as directed.
   - Record blood pressure daily at home for about one week and report results to clinician to determine whether another agent is needed.

4. **Health maintenance**
   - Annual exam.
   - Mammogram due; to be scheduled.
   - Repeat lipid panel this year.

**Patient education:**
- Patient asked whether all medications can be taken together. Advised that they can be taken at the same time. Suggested setting a daily alarm to help with adherence. Patient agreed this may help.

**Follow-up:** Not specified in transcript.

1. Right knee injury. Clinician is concerned for an MCL (medial collateral ligament) tear or injury, given the reported pop, weight-bearing difficulty, and medial tenderness.
2. Type 2 diabetes, being treated by primary care. Clinician notes she is managing it reasonably well. (Diabetes type not stated in transcript; verify.)

**Plan:**
1. Right knee:
   - Straight-leg brace.
   - Mobic prescribed for pain and swelling.
   - Ice the knee for about 15 minutes, once an hour.

2. Diabetes:
   - Recheck hemoglobin A1c.
   - Refill metformin 500 mg; continue current dose.

**Patient:** George
**Visit type:** Office visit

**Chief complaint:** Numbness and tingling in the fingers and pain in the wrist.

**History of present illness:**
- Patient reports right wrist and hand pain with numbness for several months. Onset was gradual and not linked to a known injury.
- Symptoms are worse at night. Patient sometimes wakes with the hand asleep and has to shake it out.
- Numbness involves all fingers, more prominently the thumb and index finger. The little finger is sometimes numb.
- Patient reports weakness in the left hand and dropping objects, which he attributes to reduced feeling.
- Occupation: landscaping (yard work, maintenance, flower beds). Work is heavy labor with repetitive motions (raking, digging) daily.
- Alcohol: one or two beers on Fridays and Saturdays.
- No prior diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis; patient reports no one has mentioned it.

**Review of systems:** Heart and lungs listened to; no abnormalities noted in the transcript.

**Physical exam:**
- Grip strength reduced on the left compared with the right.
- Light touch: patient feels touch in all right fingers; sensation feels "weirder" on the thumb side than the index finger side.
- Tinel's sign positive bilaterally (tingling/jolt in fingertips with percussion over the wrist on both sides).
- Vitals: not recorded in transcript.

**Assessment:** Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, per clinician's impression, with repetitive occupational activity as a likely contributor. Clinical exam and history are consistent with this impression. Diagnostic confirmation pending.

**Plan:**
1. Order EMG to assess electrical conduction in the fingers. Follow-up on results.
2. Activity modification: avoid repetitive hand and wrist motions for approximately two weeks. Patient will try to delegate heavy or repetitive tasks to other employees.
3. Wrist splint (side not specified in transcript).
4. Ibuprofen 600 mg every six hours.
5. Return to clinic in two weeks to reassess. Consider further diagnostic testing or surgical referral for release of pressure on the nerve if symptoms persist.
6. Patient agreed with the plan. Nurse to discharge patient.

- Numbness involves all fingers, more prominently the thumb and index finger. The little finger is sometimes numb.
- Patient reports weakness in the left hand and dropping objects, which he attributes to reduced feeling.
- Occupation: landscaping (yard work, maintenance, flower beds). Work is heavy labor with repetitive motions (raking, digging) daily.
- Alcohol: one or two beers on Fridays and Saturdays.
- No prior diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis; patient reports no one has mentioned it.

**Review of systems:** Heart and lungs listened to; no abnormalities noted in the transcript.

**Physical exam:**
- Grip strength reduced on the left compared with the right.
- Light touch: patient feels touch in all right fingers; sensation feels "weirder" on the thumb side than the index finger side.
- Tinel's sign positive bilaterally (tingling/jolt in fingertips with percussion over the wrist on both sides).
- Vitals: not recorded in transcript.

**Assessment:** Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, per clinician's impression, with repetitive occupational activity as a likely contributor. Clinical exam and history are consistent with this impression. Diagnostic confirmation pending.

**Plan:**
1. Order EMG to assess electrical conduction in the fingers. Follow-up on results.
2. Activity modification: avoid repetitive hand and wrist motions for approximately two weeks. Patient will try to delegate heavy or repetitive tasks to other employees.
3. Wrist splint (side not specified in transcript).
4. Ibuprofen 600 mg every six hours.
5. Return to clinic in two weeks to reassess. Consider further diagnostic testing or surgical referral for release of pressure on the nerve if symptoms persist.
6. Patient agreed with the plan. Nurse to discharge patient.
